Why round 2. Rhys found round 1 starting to repeat: the same tapered strip on every hole, doglegs one way then the other, a bunker on each side. This round gives every hole a story built round a feature of its own that shapes the play and the view, varies how the fairways are put together, and varies the sand. New rules for every course: docs/COURSE-DESIGN.md, "Story, features and fairway structure".

1 The Overlook: the creek. Camp Falls now spills off the bluff's east end and runs the length of the floor below you as a creek, crossing the 1st on a diagonal about 268 m out (nearest in the corner), so the fairway comes in two pieces. A fallen giant lies across it in the corner. All four tee sets drive short of it; the bold line carries it and the tree ferns over the corner. The landing area now leans left, away from the water.

2 Cycad Grove: the giant. A monkey-puzzle 56 m tall stands alone in the middle of the fairway at the corner, a ring of cycads round its foot, splitting it into two lanes: left, inside the corner, short and tight; right, wide and longer. A waste of sand and gravel runs 150 m down the whole right side.

3 The Tar Pit: the skeleton. A great horned skull and ribcage stand out of the largest pool, the first thing you see from the tee, and the tar now wraps the green's front and right in three pools. No sand on the hole: the tar is the hazard. The way round is still left.

4 The Floodplain: the back channel. A braid leaves the river and crosses the hole on a diagonal about 300 m out into an oxbow pond on the left, so the fairway stops short of it and starts again beyond. The river's gravel bars are the only sand until the green.

5 The Plunge Pool: the shelf. The green now fills a tongue of rock jutting out into the pool, water on three sides, the falls straight behind; the neck of the shelf, short grass, is the way on from the left.
6 The Strangler. As before: the root arch is its feature.

7 The Bone Bed: the bluff in the fairway, and a ring of sand. The Bone Bluff (30 m high, the skeleton in its face toward you) now stands in the middle of the fairway at the corner. Left of it is wide and safe but blind to the green; right, between the rock and the river, is the short way and opens the green up. The green sits inside a ring of sand with one way in, from the front left.

8 The Swamp: the stepping stones and a cross bunker. Round the corner two of the swamp's pools reach right across the second leg, leaving islands of fairway between them: the bold way hops from one to the next; the dry way goes round the left. A band of sand crosses both short of the last island.

9 The Nest: the step. A band of rock 4 m high crosses the ramp about 200 m out, broken down on the right into a rubble slope. Carry it and the ball sits on the upper shelf; come up short and the second is blind. Camp Falls now lands in its pool behind and left of the green, its stream running off the lip past the back of the green to the cascade. (This replaces the footbridge and gorge sketched in the concept: the water had to come off the bluff's east end to feed the 1st's creek.)

Fairway structures across the nine: 1 broken by a creek · 2 split by a tree · 3 none (a par 3 over tar) · 4 broken by a channel · 5 a green on a shelf · 6 a main way and a branch round the arch's foot · 7 split by a bluff · 8 stepping stones and a dry way · 9 a step across the climb. Sand: greenside pairs on 1, 2 and 4; a waste down the 2nd; none on 3; one at the 5th's neck; a target bunker on 6; a ring round the 7th; a cross bunker and a catch on 8; a catch and a pot on 9.
